prompts.title: Cold outreach email that earns a reply
prompts.description: Write a short, specific cold email with one clear ask, plus a subject line and a follow-up-ready variant.
prompts.body:
Write a cold outreach email from me to someone I have never spoken to.

About me: {{sender_background}}
Recipient: {{recipient}}
Why them specifically: {{personalization}}
What I want: {{ask}}
Tone: {{tone}}
Maximum length: {{max_words}} words for the email body.

Rules:
- Open with the specific reason I am writing to this person, not with who I am or "I hope this finds you well".
- Make exactly one ask, and make it small and easy to say yes to.
- Include one concrete detail of value to them (what they get, learn or save), not a list of my credentials.
- No flattery that could apply to anyone, no buzzwords, no fake urgency, no exclamation marks.
- If any key fact above is missing or vague, ask me up to 3 short questions first. Otherwise write straight away.

Output format:
1. Three subject lines (under 50 characters each), best first.
2. The email body, ready to send, ending with my first name only.
3. A one-sentence note on why the opening should work, so I can adjust it.

variables.label: About you
variables.default: Freelance product designer with 8 years in fintech apps.
variables.help: Who you are, in a sentence or two

variables.label: Recipient
variables.default: Priya Shah, Head of Product at a payments startup

variables.label: Why them
variables.default: She recently posted about redesigning their onboarding flow and the drop-off after ID verification.

variables.label: Your ask
variables.default: A 15-minute call to share two onboarding ideas

variables.label: Tone
variables.default: Warm and professional

prompts.exampleOutput:
Subject lines
1. Your onboarding drop-off after ID check
2. Two ideas for your verification step
3. Quick thought on your onboarding post

Email
Hi Priya,

Your post about losing users right after ID verification caught my eye. I spent the last few years fixing exactly that step in two fintech apps, and the fixes were smaller than people expect: showing progress before the camera opens, and explaining why each document is needed.

I sketched two ideas based on your public flow. Would a 15-minute call next week be useful, so I can walk you through them? If not, no worries at all, and I am happy to send the sketches by email instead.

Best,
Daniel

Why the opening works: it proves you read her post and names the exact problem she described, so it does not read as a template.
prompts.notes: Specificity in the 'why them' field is what separates this from a template. Paste a real sentence from their post or site for the best result.

prompts.title: Follow-up email when they have not replied
prompts.description: Nudge someone who went quiet without sounding pushy, with a new reason to respond and an easy way out.

variables.label: What you sent first
variables.default: I proposed a guest article swap between our two newsletters and attached three topic ideas.

variables.label: Who they are
variables.default: An editor I have met once at a conference

variables.label: What you need
variables.default: A yes or no on the article swap

variables.label: Follow-up number
variables.default: First

variables.label: Tone
variables.default: Friendly and casual

prompts.exampleOutput:
Version A (light touch)
Subject: Re: Newsletter swap

Hi Maya,

Quick one: if the swap works for you, which of the three topics would you pick? A one-word answer is enough. If the timing is off, just say so and I will leave it with you.

Thanks,
Sam

Version B (more direct)
Subject: Newsletter swap, can we lock a date?

Hi Maya,

I am planning my June issues this week and would like to hold a slot for you. Could you tell me yes or no by Friday? If it is a no, that is completely fine.

Thanks,
Sam

Recommendation: send Version A for a first follow-up. It lowers the effort of replying and keeps the tone friendly.
prompts.notes: Giving a deadline that is real (like a planning date) works far better than invented urgency. Pick Final to get a gracious close-the-loop message.

prompts.title: Email for a difficult conversation
prompts.description: Deliver hard news or feedback clearly and kindly, without burying the point or sounding cold.

variables.label: Situation
variables.default: A colleague has missed the last three deadlines on shared reports, and it is delaying my team's work.

variables.label: Recipient
variables.default: A peer I get along with, Chris, from the analytics team

variables.label: Desired outcome
variables.default: Agree a realistic delivery schedule this week

variables.label: Do not say
variables.default: Do not mention performance reviews or escalate to his manager

variables.label: Tone
variables.default: Empathetic

prompts.exampleOutput:
Subject: Report timing and finding a schedule that works

Hi Chris,

I want to raise something directly: the last three shared reports have arrived after the agreed dates, and that has pushed back my team's analysis each time.

I know your plate is full, and I would rather solve this with you than around you. Could we agree on delivery dates that are realistic for you? I am flexible on format if that makes it easier.

Can we spend 20 minutes on Thursday to work it out? Tell me what time suits you.

Thanks,
Alex

Riskiest phrase: "have arrived after the agreed dates". Softer: "have landed later than we planned".

Call or email: A short call would likely land better; use this email only as a written follow-up to confirm the new dates.
prompts.notes: The 'riskiest phrase' check catches wording that triggers defensiveness. Listing what you must not say keeps the draft clear of promises you cannot keep.

prompts.title: Tighten a draft without changing its meaning
prompts.description: Cut filler and repetition from your draft while keeping your voice, with a log of what changed.
prompts.body:
Edit the draft below to make it tighter and clearer without changing its meaning or voice.

Type of writing: {{doc_type}}
Reader: {{audience}}
Target length: {{target}}

Draft:
{{draft}}

Rules:
- Remove filler, repeated points, hedging and throat-clearing. Prefer short words and active verbs.
- Keep my facts, numbers, names and any quoted text exactly as written.
- Keep my voice. Do not make it more formal, more upbeat or more generic than the original.
- Do not add new claims or ideas.
- If a sentence is ambiguous, keep it close to the original and flag it instead of guessing.

Output format:
1. The edited draft.
2. Word count before and after.
3. A short list (maximum 5 bullets) of the most important changes and why.
4. Any sentences you flagged as unclear.

variables.label: Type of writing
variables.default: Internal project update email

variables.label: Reader
variables.default: Senior leaders who skim

variables.label: Target length
variables.default: About 30% shorter

variables.label: Your draft
variables.default: I just wanted to take a moment to give everyone a quick update on where we are currently at with the migration project. As of right now, we have basically finished moving about 80 percent of the services over to the new platform, and we are really on track to be done by the end of June, although there are a couple of risks that we should keep an eye on.

prompts.exampleOutput:
Edited draft
Update on the migration: 80% of services are now on the new platform, and we are on track to finish by the end of June. A couple of risks need watching.

Word count: 62 before, 34 after.

Main changes
- Removed the opening phrase ("I just wanted to take a moment") because it delays the news.
- Cut "basically", "really", "currently" and "as of right now"; they add no information.
- Merged two sentences so the status and the date arrive together.
- Shortened the risk sentence; the risks themselves can follow in a separate line.

Flagged
- "A couple of risks": the reader will want to know what they are. Consider listing them.
prompts.notes: The flag step stops the model from quietly inventing details. Re-run with a stricter target, such as 'half the length', for a second pass.

prompts.title: Rewrite any text in a different tone
prompts.description: Shift a message's tone, from blunt to warm or casual to formal, while preserving every fact.
prompts.body:
Rewrite the text below so it sounds {{target_tone}}, for {{audience}}.

Original text:
{{text}}

Current tone, in my own words: {{current_tone}}

Rules:
- Keep all facts, numbers, dates, names and requests unchanged.
- Change vocabulary, sentence length, openings and sign-offs to fit the new tone. Do not just swap in a few adjectives.
- Avoid clichés and filler such as "I hope this email finds you well" or "touch base".
- Keep the length within 15% of the original unless the tone needs more or less.
- Do not add emojis unless the target tone is casual and the original already uses them.

Output format:
1. The rewritten text.
2. Two bullets on the main stylistic choices you made.
3. One alternative opening sentence for people who want a different feel.

variables.label: Target tone
variables.default: warm and respectful

variables.label: Audience
variables.default: A long-term client

variables.label: Current tone
variables.default: Curt and a bit annoyed

variables.label: Text to rewrite
variables.default: We need the signed contract by Friday. This is the third time I have asked. Without it we cannot start the work and the schedule will slip.

prompts.exampleOutput:
Rewritten text
Hi, thank you again for your patience while we sort out the paperwork. To keep your project on schedule, we would be grateful to have the signed contract by Friday. Without it we are not able to begin, and I would hate for the timeline to slip. If anything about the contract is holding things up, tell me and I will happily help.

Style choices
- Replaced the count of requests with an appreciation line to remove blame.
- Gave the reason for the deadline as a shared goal (protecting their schedule) and offered help.

Alternative opening
"I wanted to follow up on the contract so we can get your project started on time."
prompts.notes: Describing the current tone helps the model know what to undo. For brand voice, paste a sample paragraph of your own writing into the audience field.

prompts.title: Turn rough notes into a blog post
prompts.description: Convert scattered notes into a structured, readable blog post in your voice, without padding or invented facts.

variables.label: Topic
variables.default: Why small teams should write down decisions

variables.label: Reader
variables.default: Startup founders and team leads with no formal process

variables.label: Goal
variables.default: Convince readers to start a simple decision log this week

variables.label: Voice
variables.default: Conversational and practical

variables.label: Search phrase
variables.default: decision log

variables.label: Your notes
variables.default:
- we kept re-arguing the same pricing choice every quarter
- a one-page doc per decision: context, options, choice, date
- took 10 minutes each, saved hours
- new hires onboarded faster
- don't aim for perfect, aim for findable

prompts.exampleOutput:
Title: Write Down Your Decisions (It Takes Ten Minutes)
Meta: A simple decision log stops teams re-arguing old choices. Here is a one-page format you can start this week.

Every quarter, my team re-argued the same pricing decision. Nobody was wrong; nobody could remember why we had chosen what we chose.

## The fix is one page
For each decision, write four things: the context, the options considered, what you chose, and the date. That is it.

## Ten minutes, hours saved
Each entry took about ten minutes. It saved far more by ending repeat debates before they began.

## A bonus: faster onboarding
New hires read the log and understood our reasoning without a dozen meetings.

## Aim for findable, not perfect
[add data: how many decisions you logged in the first quarter]

Start this week: pick the last decision you argued about twice and write it up.

Placeholders to fill: one data point in "Aim for findable".
prompts.notes: The placeholder rule keeps the draft honest. Add your own anecdotes in the notes for a post that does not read like generic content.

prompts.title: Headline and title variants by angle
prompts.description: Generate sharp headlines grouped by angle, each under a length limit, with a pick for your goal.
prompts.body:
Write headline options for the piece below.

What it is: {{content_type}}
What it is about: {{summary}}
Reader: {{audience}}
Main goal: {{goal}}
Maximum characters per headline: {{max_chars}}

Create 12 headlines, three for each of these angles:
1. Clear and literal (says exactly what the reader gets)
2. Curiosity (a gap the reader wants to close, without hiding the topic)
3. Benefit or outcome (a specific result, with a number if the summary supports one)
4. Contrarian or surprising (challenges a common belief that is true to the content)

Rules:
- Stay accurate. Do not promise anything the piece does not deliver.
- No clickbait formulas such as "You won't believe" or "This one trick".
- Vary structure and opening words.
- Stay within the character limit and show the character count of each.

Output format: a table with columns Angle, Headline, Characters. Then name your top pick for the stated goal and explain it in one sentence.

variables.label: Content type
variables.default: Blog post

variables.label: Summary
variables.default: A practical guide to running 30-minute weekly one-on-ones that managers keep and employees value, with a simple agenda and three questions to ask.

variables.label: Reader
variables.default: New people managers

variables.label: Goal
variables.default: Clicks from search

prompts.exampleOutput:
| Angle | Headline | Characters |
|---|---|---|
| Clear | How to Run a 30-Minute One-on-One That Works | 44 |
| Clear | A Simple Agenda for Weekly One-on-Ones | 38 |
| Clear | One-on-One Meetings: A Guide for New Managers | 45 |
| Curiosity | The Three Questions Great Managers Always Ask | 45 |
| Curiosity | Why Your One-on-Ones Keep Getting Cancelled | 43 |
| Curiosity | What Employees Actually Want From a One-on-One | 46 |
| Benefit | Run One-on-Ones People Keep in 30 Minutes a Week | 48 |
| Benefit | 3 Questions That Turn Check-Ins Into Real Talk | 46 |
| Benefit | A One-on-One Agenda You Can Use Tomorrow | 40 |
| Contrarian | Stop Using One-on-Ones for Status Updates | 41 |
| Contrarian | Your One-on-One Is Not Your Meeting | 35 |
| Contrarian | Shorter One-on-Ones Get Better Results | 38 |

Top pick for search clicks: "How to Run a 30-Minute One-on-One That Works", because it matches how people search and states the payoff.
prompts.notes: Choosing the goal changes which headlines rise to the top. Ask for a second round on the angle you like best.

prompts.title: Executive summary for busy decision-makers
prompts.description: Condense a long report or document into a one-page summary that leads with the decision needed.
prompts.body:
Write an executive summary of the document below for {{reader}}.

What the document is: {{doc_type}}
Decision or action the reader needs to take: {{decision}}
Length limit: {{length}}

Document:
{{document}}

Rules:
- Lead with the conclusion or recommendation, then the reasons. Do not follow the document's order.
- Keep the numbers that drive the decision and drop the rest. Do not round or alter figures.
- State risks, costs and open questions plainly. Do not make the case sound stronger than the source does.
- Do not add information that is not in the document. If something important is missing, say so under "Gaps".
- Plain language; define any jargon the reader may not know.

Output format:
**Bottom line** (2 sentences)
**Why** (3-5 bullets)
**Risks and unknowns** (2-4 bullets)
**What I need from you** (1-2 lines)
**Gaps in the source** (only if relevant)

variables.label: Reader
variables.default: The COO, who has five minutes

variables.label: Document type
variables.default: Quarterly operations review

variables.label: Decision needed
variables.default: Approve extra budget for a second warehouse shift

variables.label: Length
variables.default: Under 200 words

variables.label: Document text
variables.default: Q3 order volume rose 24% versus Q2. On-time shipping fell from 96% to 89%, mostly in the last two weeks of each month. Overtime cost rose to $118k from $64k. A second shift would cost about $210k per quarter, and would restore on-time shipping to 95% by modelling. Customer complaints about delays doubled. We have not yet confirmed hiring capacity.

prompts.exampleOutput:
**Bottom line**
Add a second warehouse shift. Shipping reliability is slipping as volume grows, and overtime is already costing more than half of what a second shift would.

**Why**
- Orders grew 24% in Q3; on-time shipping fell from 96% to 89%.
- Overtime rose from $64k to $118k.
- Modelling shows a second shift (about $210k per quarter) restores on-time rates to 95%.
- Complaints about delays doubled.

**Risks and unknowns**
- Hiring capacity is not yet confirmed.
- The 95% figure is modelled, not observed.

**What I need from you**
Approve the budget in principle, conditional on a hiring plan.

**Gaps in the source**
No customer churn data linked to the delays.
prompts.notes: Stating the decision up front shapes the whole summary around what the reader must do. The Gaps section makes missing evidence visible instead of papered over.

prompts.title: Plain-language rewrite for any reader
prompts.description: Rewrite dense, technical or legal text so a general reader understands it, without losing accuracy.
prompts.body:
Rewrite the text below in plain language for {{audience}}.

Reading level target: {{reading_level}}
Purpose of the text: {{purpose}}

Text:
{{text}}

Rules:
- Keep the meaning exact. Do not drop conditions, exceptions, deadlines, amounts or obligations.
- Use short sentences, everyday words and active voice. Put the most important thing first.
- Replace jargon with plain words. If a technical term must stay, explain it once in brackets.
- Address the reader as "you" where the text speaks to them.
- Use a short list for steps or requirements.
- If something is ambiguous in the source, do not resolve it by guessing. Mark it with [unclear in source: ...].

Output format:
1. The plain-language version.
2. A glossary of terms you replaced or explained (term: plain meaning).
3. A short "What changed in meaning?" statement, which should say "Nothing" unless you had to make a judgment call.

variables.label: Audience
variables.default: Customers with no legal background

variables.label: Reading level
variables.default: Grade 8

variables.label: Purpose
variables.default: Explain a cancellation policy

variables.label: Text
variables.default: Subscriber may terminate this Agreement upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice. Fees paid in respect of the then-current billing period shall be non-refundable, notwithstanding any termination hereunder, save where termination is occasioned by the Provider's uncured material breach.

prompts.exampleOutput:
Plain-language version
You can cancel at any time. Tell us in writing at least 30 days before you want to stop.

If you cancel, we do not refund what you have already paid for the current billing period. There is one exception: if we seriously broke our agreement with you and did not fix the problem, you can get that money back.

Glossary
- Terminate: cancel
- Prior written notice: telling us in writing ahead of time
- Material breach: a serious failure to keep the agreement
- Uncured: not fixed

What changed in meaning?
Nothing. "Uncured" is shown as "did not fix the problem"; the source does not say how long we have to fix it.
prompts.notes: The meaning-check step guards against oversimplification. For anything legally binding, have a professional review the plain version before you publish it.

prompts.title: Article outline with a clear argument
prompts.description: Build a structured outline with a thesis, section goals and evidence to gather before you start drafting.

variables.label: Topic
variables.default: The hidden cost of constant meetings for remote teams

variables.label: Format
variables.default: Long-form blog article

variables.label: Reader
variables.default: Remote team leads who already feel overloaded by calendar invites

variables.label: Your point
variables.default: Most meeting overload is a documentation problem, not a scheduling problem

variables.label: Your material
variables.default: One story about cutting my team's meetings by 40%; a survey stat I half-remember; nothing else yet.

prompts.exampleOutput:
Thesis: Most meeting overload is a documentation problem, not a scheduling problem.

1. The hook: the calendar that eats a week (150 words)
Purpose: make the pain concrete.
- Open with the 40% cut story, starting from the before state.
- NEEDS: exact hours per week the team reclaimed.

2. Why we blame scheduling (200 words)
Purpose: explain the common fix and why it fails.
- Focus time blocks, no-meeting days.
- Why people still end up in meetings.

3. What meetings are really doing (300 words)
Purpose: prove the thesis.
- Meetings as a substitute for missing written context.
- Three kinds of meetings that disappear once something is documented.
- NEEDS: survey stat with source.

4. Counterargument: some talks must be live (200 words)
- Answer: separate decisions from updates.

5. How to start (400 words)
6. Conclusion (150 words)

NEEDS by priority: survey source; hours reclaimed; one outside expert quote.
prompts.notes: The NEEDS tags turn the outline into a research to-do list. Paste the outline back after research and ask for a draft one section at a time.

prompts.title: Honest editor critique of your draft
prompts.description: Get a prioritized, specific critique of structure, clarity and persuasion, with fixes you can apply.

variables.label: Type
variables.default: Opinion essay

variables.label: Reader
variables.default: General readers of a business magazine

variables.label: Goal
variables.default: Persuade readers that four-day weeks are worth trying

variables.label: Your worry
variables.default: It feels preachy and a bit long

variables.label: Draft
variables.default: Everyone knows that work is broken. We are all tired, and companies need to do something about it. Four-day weeks are the answer. Many studies have shown that they work. Employees are happier and more productive. Companies should try them. In conclusion, the four-day week is the future of work.

prompts.exampleOutput:
Verdict
The position is clear, but the draft asserts rather than shows. It leans on broad claims ("everyone knows", "many studies") with no evidence, which is why it reads as preachy.

Strengths
- A clear, committed thesis.
- Short sentences that are easy to follow.

Fix first
1. "Many studies have shown that they work." Name one study, with a result. A single concrete figure beats this sentence.
2. "Everyone knows that work is broken." Replace with a specific scene, such as a Friday-afternoon inbox, to earn the reader's agreement.

Fix next
3. Add the strongest objection (coverage, customer service) and answer it.

Polish
4. "In conclusion" is unnecessary; end on the trial you propose.

Score: 5/10. The single change that raises it most: replace the generic claims with one real company's results.
prompts.notes: Sharing your worry steers attention, but the fixed checklist keeps the critique balanced. Ask a follow-up like 'rewrite my first paragraph using your fixes'.

prompts.title: Meeting notes to a clear recap email
prompts.description: Turn messy meeting notes or a transcript into decisions, action items with owners, and a shareable recap.

variables.label: Meeting
variables.default: Website relaunch weekly sync

variables.label: Date
variables.default: 14 March

variables.label: Recipients
variables.default: The project team and the marketing director

variables.label: Tone
variables.default: Direct and concise

variables.label: Notes
variables.default: launch date moved from 3 April to 17 April bc dev is behind on checkout. Jo to finish checkout by 5 April. we talked about homepage copy, not final. Sam will get legal to review the privacy page. budget fine for now. unclear if we need extra QA time, ask Lee. next sync same time next week.

Subject: Website relaunch sync, 14 March: decisions and actions

Hi all,

Decisions
- Launch moves from 3 April to 17 April because checkout development is behind.

Action items
| Task | Owner | Due |

prompts.title: Politely decline a request
prompts.description: Say no clearly and kindly to a request or invitation, protecting the relationship and your time.

variables.label: The request
variables.default: Join a panel at a conference in October

variables.label: Who asked
variables.default: An organiser I met last year, friendly but not close

variables.label: Reason
variables.default: My calendar is full through the autumn

variables.label: Alternative
variables.default: Recommend a colleague who speaks on the same topic

variables.label: Tone
variables.default: Warm and professional

variables.label: Channel
variables.default: Email

prompts.exampleOutput:
Hi Elena,

Thank you for thinking of me for the October panel. I am not able to take it on, as my calendar is full through the autumn.

If it is helpful, I would suggest Marcus Webb, who speaks on the same topic and would be a great fit. I am happy to introduce you.

I hope the event goes brilliantly.

Best,
Jordan

Firmer first sentences
1. "Thank you for the invitation, but I have to decline the October panel."
2. "I will not be able to join the October panel."

prompts.title: LinkedIn post that sounds like a person
prompts.description: Turn an experience or lesson into an engaging LinkedIn post with a strong first line and no cringe.

variables.label: Your story
variables.default: I rejected a promotion to stay as an individual contributor. My manager was surprised, and for a week I questioned myself.

variables.label: Takeaway
variables.default: Growth does not have to mean managing people

variables.label: Role and audience
variables.default: Senior engineer writing for other engineers

variables.label: Voice
variables.default: Plainspoken and honest

variables.label: Length
variables.default: Medium (150-200 words)

prompts.exampleOutput:
I turned down a promotion last month.

My manager was surprised. For a week, so was I.

Everyone around me seemed to treat the management track as the only way up. But when I pictured the job, I saw fewer hours writing code and more hours in calendars. I like building things. I like mentoring one-on-one. I did not want to give that up for a title.

What helped was asking a different question: not "what is the next level?" but "what work do I want more of in two years?"

I am staying as a senior engineer, and I have asked to lead more technical design work instead.

Growth does not have to mean managing people.

Has anyone else had to choose between the title and the work?

Alternative first lines
1. "My manager was surprised when I said no to the promotion."
2. "I walked away from a bigger title last month."
prompts.notes: The 'use only my details' rule stops made-up statistics. Real, specific stories outperform advice, so keep the story field concrete.

prompts.title: Tailored cover letter from your real experience
prompts.description: Write a specific, credible cover letter that links your experience to the role, without clichés.

variables.label: Role and company
variables.default: Customer Success Manager at Lumen Analytics

variables.label: Job description highlights
variables.default: Own onboarding for mid-market accounts; reduce churn; work with product on feedback; strong written communication.

variables.label: Your experience
variables.default: 4 years in customer support and then success at a SaaS company. Built an onboarding checklist that cut time-to-first-value from 21 to 12 days. Handled a 60-account portfolio with 94% renewal. Wrote the weekly product feedback digest.

variables.label: Why this company
variables.default: I use Lumen's dashboards and like how they explain data to non-analysts

variables.label: Tone
variables.default: Confident and persuasive

prompts.exampleOutput:
Dear Hiring Team,

Cutting the time customers need to see value from three weeks to under two is the kind of result I would like to bring to Lumen Analytics.

In my current role, I built an onboarding checklist that reduced time-to-first-value from 21 to 12 days. For mid-market onboarding, that experience matters: customers who succeed early are far more likely to stay. I manage a 60-account portfolio with a 94% renewal rate, which taught me to spot churn risk early and keep communication specific.

You also ask for work with product. Each week I write a product feedback digest that turns customer conversations into clear, prioritised requests for the product team.

I use Lumen's dashboards, and I admire how they explain data to people who are not analysts. I would love to help your customers get the same clarity.

I would welcome a conversation about how I can help your onboarding team.

Sincerely,
[Name]

Gaps to prepare for: no mention of mid-market account size; be ready to discuss it.
prompts.notes: Paste real numbers into your experience; the letter is only as persuasive as the evidence. The gap list is a free interview-prep checklist.

prompts.title: Proofread without flattening your voice
prompts.description: Fix grammar, spelling and punctuation while leaving your style and word choices alone.
prompts.body:
Proofread the text below. Fix errors only; do not rewrite.

Language and spelling convention: {{variety}}
Style rules to follow, if any: {{style_rules}}

Text:
{{text}}

Rules:
- Correct spelling, grammar, punctuation, capitalisation, typos and obvious word errors (such as "their" vs "there").
- Do NOT change word choice, rhythm, tone, or sentence structure unless a sentence is genuinely ungrammatical.
- Do not touch quotations, names, code or intentional stylistic choices such as fragments, unless they are clearly mistakes.
- Make consistent decisions: hyphenation, numerals, serial commas and capitalisation should match throughout.
- If something might be an error but could be intentional, leave it and list it as a query.

Output format:
1. The corrected text.
2. A change log table: Original, Corrected, Reason.
3. Queries: items for me to decide.

variables.label: Spelling
variables.default: US English

variables.label: Style rules
variables.default: Use the serial comma; spell out numbers under ten

variables.label: Text
variables.default: Their are three things we learnt from the launch. First, customers dont read long emails, they skim. Second, the pricing page confused alot of people. Third: we should of tested the checkout earlier.

prompts.exampleOutput:
Corrected text
There are three things we learned from the launch. First, customers don't read long emails; they skim. Second, the pricing page confused a lot of people. Third, we should have tested the checkout earlier.

Change log
| Original | Corrected | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Their are | There are | Wrong word |
| learnt | learned | US spelling |
| dont | don't | Missing apostrophe |
| emails, they | emails; they | Comma splice |
| alot | a lot | Spelling |
| Third: | Third, | Matches "First," and "Second," |
| should of | should have | Grammar |

Queries
- "three things" are spelled out, which matches your rule; confirm "launch" should be lower case.
prompts.notes: Choosing the language variety prevents silent switches between UK and US spelling. Add your house style rules for consistency across documents.

prompts.title: Draft a reply to an email you received
prompts.description: Paste an incoming email and your intent, and get a reply that answers every point in the right tone.

variables.label: Their email
variables.default: Hi, we are interested in your team workshop. Can you do June 12 in Leeds? How many people can attend and what is the price? Also, do you provide materials in advance?

variables.label: Your points
variables.default: Yes to June 12 in Leeds. Max 20 people. 2,400 pounds plus travel. Slides are shared a week before.

variables.label: Relationship
variables.default: Potential new client, first contact

variables.label: Tone
variables.default: Warm and professional

variables.label: Length
variables.default: Short

prompts.exampleOutput:
Hi,

Thanks for getting in touch. Here are the answers to your questions.

- Date and location: June 12 in Leeds works for us.
- Group size: the workshop is best with up to 20 attendees.
- Price: 2,400 pounds, plus travel costs.
- Materials: we share the slides one week before the session.

If this suits you, tell me the final number of attendees and I will send a booking confirmation this week.

Best regards,
[Your name]

Unanswered items
- No question was left unanswered. You may wish to confirm venue arrangements and who covers room hire.
prompts.notes: Giving rough points rather than full sentences works best. The unanswered list prevents silent commitments.

prompts.title: Weekly status update for your manager
prompts.description: Turn your week's work into a crisp status update covering progress, blockers and next steps.

variables.label: Reader
variables.default: My director, who reads this on her phone

variables.label: Project
variables.default: Mobile app v2.0 rebuild

variables.label: Period
variables.default: Week of 9 June

variables.label: Format
variables.default: Slack message

variables.label: Raw notes
variables.default: finished login screens, 12 of 15 screens done. payments API still not ready from vendor, waiting since Tuesday. QA found 4 crash bugs, 3 fixed. thinking release may slip if payments not here by 20 June. next: finish remaining screens, start load test.
variables.help: Anything you did, in any order

prompts.exampleOutput:
**Status: At risk.** Release depends on the vendor's payments API, which has not arrived.

**Done**
- 12 of 15 screens complete, including login.
- QA found 4 crash bugs; 3 are fixed.

**Blockers and asks**
- Payments API from the vendor, outstanding since Tuesday. Release slips if it is not delivered by 20 June. Could you escalate to the vendor contact?

prompts.notes: Marking an honest At risk with a named ask is what makes a status update useful. Include dates in your notes for sharper deadlines.

prompts.title: Customer apology that fixes the problem
prompts.description: Reply to an unhappy customer with a sincere, specific apology and a clear remedy, not canned phrases.

variables.label: Customer message
variables.default: I ordered a standing desk three weeks ago for a delivery date that you confirmed. It still hasn't arrived and nobody answers my emails. I am working from my kitchen table because of this.

variables.label: What happened
variables.default: Carrier lost the parcel; our support inbox backlog meant emails went unanswered for 5 days

variables.label: What we can offer
variables.default: Free express replacement shipped tomorrow with tracking, plus a 15% refund

variables.label: What we cannot do
variables.default: Cannot guarantee a delivery date, only dispatch date

variables.label: Brand voice
variables.default: Warm and professional

variables.label: Channel
variables.default: Email

prompts.exampleOutput:
Hi Jordan,

I am sorry. You were promised a delivery date, the desk never arrived, and your emails went unanswered for days. Both failures are ours.

The carrier lost your parcel, and our support inbox fell behind. That should not have left you working from the kitchen table.

Here is what we are doing: a replacement desk ships by express tomorrow, with tracking sent to you the moment it dispatches. We are also refunding 15% of your order today. I cannot promise the exact delivery date, but I will personally watch the shipment and write to you as soon as it moves.

You can reach me directly at this address.

Sincerely,
Alex, Customer Care

Biggest risk: "Both failures are ours" admits fault in writing. If legal review is needed, use "this should have been handled better".
prompts.notes: Supplying real internal facts allows an honest explanation rather than a canned one. Keep the 'cannot do' field filled so the reply never overpromises.

prompts.title: Stress-test an argument or persuasive piece
prompts.description: Find the weak points in your reasoning: gaps, unsupported claims, counterarguments and how to repair each.
prompts.body:
Review the argument below like a sharp, fair critic who wants it to succeed.

The argument or piece:
{{argument}}

Who needs to be convinced: {{audience}}
What they currently believe: {{audience_belief}}
How rigorous to be: {{rigor}}

Assess and report on:
1. The core claim, restated in one sentence, and whether it matches what I seem to intend.
2. Each key premise, marked as supported, plausible but unsupported, or doubtful.
3. Logical gaps or leaps, including any fallacies (name them, quote the line).
4. The three strongest objections this audience would raise, ranked by how damaging they are.
5. Evidence I should add, specifically what kind and where it would go.
6. What the piece does well and should keep.

Rules:
- Quote the lines you are critiquing. Be specific and concise.
- Do not invent facts or studies. If you suggest evidence, describe the type, not fake citations.
- Do not argue the opposite position for its own sake; focus on making this argument stronger.

Output format: use the six numbered headings, then a prioritized repair list of at most five steps.

variables.label: Your argument
variables.default: Cities should ban cars from downtown centers. Cars cause pollution and noise. Cities like Oslo have done similar things and are better for it. Shops will do better because more people walk. The only people opposed are those who don't care about the environment.

variables.label: Audience
variables.default: City councillors and local business owners

variables.label: Their current view
variables.default: Skeptical; worried about lost customers

variables.label: Rigor
variables.default: Thorough

prompts.exampleOutput:
1. Core claim
Cities should ban cars from downtown centers because it improves environment and commerce.

2. Premises
- Cars cause pollution and noise: supported (widely accepted).
- Oslo's experience proves success: plausible but unsupported; no outcome data given.
- Shops do better with more walkers: doubtful for this audience; unsupported.

3. Gaps
- "The only people opposed are those who don't care about the environment" is a straw man; it dismisses real concerns about deliveries and access.

4. Likely objections
1. Loss of customers who drive in.
2. Delivery and disability access.
3. Oslo's context differs from ours.

5. Evidence to add
Retail sales data from pedestrianised streets, with before/after comparisons.

6. Keep
A clear position and a concrete example.

Repair list: replace the straw man, add sales evidence, address access.
prompts.notes: Naming the audience's current belief matters: the best objections come from their point of view. Run it again after revising to see if issues are fixed.

prompts.title: Extract claims and facts to verify
prompts.description: Pull every checkable claim, number and quote from a piece into a fact-check list with a priority and source type.
prompts.body:
Read the text below and build a fact-checking list.

Text:
{{text}}

What the text is for: {{purpose}}
Publication standard: {{standard}}

Extract every statement that can be checked: statistics, dates, named people and organisations, quotations, causal claims, superlatives ("first", "largest") and attributed opinions.

For each item provide:
- The exact wording from the text, in quotes.
- Claim type (statistic, quote, date, attribution, causal claim, superlative, other).
- Risk if wrong: High, Medium or Low (High if it could mislead readers, damage someone's reputation, or has legal implications).
- What kind of source would verify it (for example official statistics, original study, primary document, direct confirmation from the person).

Rules:
- Do not state whether claims are true. You may note that a claim looks unusually precise or is missing a source.
- Do not invent sources or links.
- Order the list by risk, High first.

Output format: a table with columns #, Claim, Type, Risk, Verify with. Then a short list of claims in the text that have no source cited.

variables.label: Text
variables.default: A 2023 study found that remote workers are 13% more productive. Our survey of 2,000 employees showed that 87% want to keep working from home. CEO Sam Park said, "Office work is dead." Remote work has caused a boom in small-town housing prices.

variables.label: Purpose
variables.default: Blog post for a general business audience

variables.label: Standard
variables.default: Standard editorial

prompts.exampleOutput:
| # | Claim | Type | Risk | Verify with |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | "Office work is dead" (attributed to CEO Sam Park) | Quote | High | Direct confirmation or original transcript |
| 2 | "Remote work has caused a boom in small-town housing prices" | Causal claim | High | Housing market data with analysis of cause |
| 3 | "A 2023 study found that remote workers are 13% more productive" | Statistic | Medium | The original study, including sample and definition |
| 4 | "87% want to keep working from home" | Statistic | Medium | Survey methodology and questionnaire |
| 5 | "survey of 2,000 employees" | Statistic | Low | Internal survey records |

Claims with no source cited
- #1 (no date or venue for the quote)
- #2 (no data, and causation asserted)
- #3 (study not named)
prompts.notes: This works as a pre-publication checklist for writers and editors. It deliberately does not judge truth, since a model cannot verify claims reliably on its own.
